title: Transfer: Subsets When the Input Has Duplicates
oneLiner: Every distinct subset of a list that may repeat values, each exactly once: the same backtracking, plus one rule about equal siblings.
keyTakeaway: Sort first, so equal values sit side by side. Then at one level of the recursion, after trying nums[i] as the next element, skip any later nums[j] equal to it (j > start and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]): it would grow exactly the same subtree again. Going deeper with an equal value is still allowed, which is how [2, 2] gets built.
explanation:
This follows Generate All Subsets with the requirement changed: nums may contain repeated values, and the answer must list every distinct subset exactly once. For [1, 2, 2] that is [], [1], [2], [1, 2], [2, 2] and [1, 2, 2]: six subsets, not the eight that treating the two 2s as different would give. Order doesn't matter; the tests sort each subset and then the list before comparing.

Run the parent lesson's code on [1, 2, 2] and you get [2] twice and [1, 2] twice. Look at where they come from: at the top level the loop tries index 1 (the first 2) and then index 2 (the second 2) as the next element. Both choices start with the same value and have the same options after them, so they grow identical subtrees.

The fix is one line in the loop, after sorting nums so equal values are neighbours: inside backtrack(start), skip index i when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]. In words: at this level, only the first copy of a value may be chosen next. The condition is i > start, not i > 0, so the second 2 can still be added right after the first one, one level deeper; that branch is how [2, 2] and [1, 2, 2] appear. Everything else (record a copy, choose, recurse with i + 1, undo) is unchanged.

Removing duplicates at the end with a set of sorted tuples also gives the right answer, but it still builds every repeated subtree first. With [2, 2, 2, 2, 2] that is 32 subsets built to keep 6. Skipping while you recurse never builds them. The worst case is still O(n · 2ⁿ) when all values differ.

The visualization runs [1, 2, 2] and shows the call stack, including the branches that are skipped.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences comparing this with Generate All Subsets. Why does skipping an equal sibling never lose a subset, why must the test be i > start rather than i > 0, and why does sorting have to happen first?

recognitionSignals: "All unique subsets" or "all unique combinations" when the input can contain repeated values.
Generating everything is the job, but equal elements would otherwise produce the same answer more than once.
gotchas: Sort before recursing; the skip rule only works when equal values are adjacent.
Skip when i > start, not i > 0: the second copy of a value must still be usable one level deeper, or [2, 2] is lost.
As in the parent lesson, record a copy of current, not current itself.
confusableWith: Backtracking: Generate All Subsets assumes distinct values, so every branch is a new subset. Here two branches can be the same subset, and the sorted skip rule prunes the second one.
3Sum skips equal neighbours for the same reason: sorted input turns "don't repeat an answer" into "don't start from the same value twice at one position".

complexity.note: When every value differs there are 2ⁿ subsets and copying each costs up to n; repeats only prune branches. Sorting is O(n log n), which is less. The recursion is at most n deep; the output itself is O(n · 2ⁿ).

referenceSolutions.python:
def subsets_with_dup(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    result = []
    current = []

    def backtrack(start):
        result.append(current[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            # An equal value already tried at this level would grow the same subtree.
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                continue
            current.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1)
            current.pop()

    backtrack(0)
    return result
